lead: Network topology is the physical layout of devices and links in a network. It decides how many cables are needed, how data travels, and how resilient the network is to failures. Different layouts suit different scales: a small office may use a star, a campus may use a partial mesh, and a data centre often combines star and mesh. Understanding each topology helps you choose the right design for cost, performance and fault‑tolerance.
prereq: You need: Data communication components and data flow modes and Network types and categories.

blocks.text: In a bus topology all nodes share a single communication line called the backbone. Each node taps the line and listens for frames addressed to it. The idea is simple: one cable, many devices, low material cost. It works well for small LANs where the total traffic is low.

items: Only one transmission at a time; CSMA/CD is used to detect and resolve collisions.
If the backbone fails, the whole network stops working.
Maximum length limited by signal attenuation; repeaters or Ethernet switches can be used to extend the network segment, but modern designs prefer switches.

blocks.where: C_total is the total usable bandwidth of the bus; C_link is the bandwidth of the single shared link.

items: Place the coaxial cable across the office.
Connect each computer with a T‑connector.
Terminate both ends with a 50 Ω resistor to prevent signal reflections.

blocks.text: A star topology connects every end device to a central hub or switch. The central node handles all traffic, making the layout easy to manage and troubleshoot. A tree (or hierarchical star) adds multiple layers of switches, creating branches that reduce cable length in large buildings.

items: Each link can operate at full duplex when a switch is used; hubs operate in half‑duplex.
Failure of one link isolates only the attached device; the rest of the network stays up.
Common in Ethernet LANs and campus networks.

blocks.where: C_agg is the aggregate bandwidth the hub can handle; N is the number of attached devices; C_link is the bandwidth of each individual link.

blocks.text: The aggregate bandwidth is limited by the switching fabric; a non‑blocking switch can support N × C_link, otherwise the actual capacity may be lower.

items: Install a managed switch in the server room.
Run Cat6 cables from the switch to each workstation.
Configure VLANs on the switch if logical segmentation is needed.

blocks.text: In a ring topology each node connects to exactly two neighbours, forming a closed loop. Frames travel in one or both directions; token passing avoids collisions. Mesh topology provides multiple redundant paths between nodes. A full mesh has a direct link for every pair, while a partial mesh connects only selected pairs.

items: Ring offers deterministic latency but a single break isolates the whole network.
Full mesh gives the highest fault tolerance; partial mesh balances cost and resilience.
Data‑centre fabrics often use a leaf‑spine partial mesh.

blocks.where: L_mesh is the number of links in a full mesh; n is the number of nodes.

items: Number the nodes from 1 to n.
Connect each node to its two neighbours to form a ring.
Add extra links between selected pairs to create a partial mesh.

examples.question: A small office has 5 computers connected in a star topology to a 100 Mbps Ethernet switch. Each computer sends data continuously to the switch. Compute (a) the total traffic arriving at the switch and (b) the maximum aggregate traffic the switch can forward if it operates in full‑duplex mode.
steps: There are 5 links, so total incoming traffic = 5 × 100 Mbps = 500 Mbps.
In full‑duplex, the switch can send 100 Mbps on each of the 5 outgoing links simultaneously.
Maximum aggregate outbound traffic = 5 × 100 Mbps = 500 Mbps.
examples.answer: The switch sees 500 Mbps of incoming traffic and can forward up to 500 Mbps outbound, assuming full‑duplex operation.
examples.check:
total = 5 * 100
print(total)
print(total)  # outbound equals inbound in full‑duplex

traps: Using n×(n‑1) instead of n(n‑1)/2 for the number of links in a full mesh gives twice the correct count.
Adding the bandwidth of all links in a star and then multiplying by 2 assumes half‑duplex; the trap is forgetting that full‑duplex allows simultaneous send and receive on each link.
Confusing a bus’s total bandwidth C_total with the per‑link bandwidth; the bus shares a single bandwidth among all nodes.
Treating a ring as having two independent paths without considering the token‑passing protocol, which limits simultaneous transmissions.

quiz.q: Name the topology where every node is connected to a single central device.
Explain why a single cable failure in a bus topology disables the whole network.
quiz.a: All nodes share the same physical medium; if the cable breaks, the electrical path is broken for every node, so no frames can be transmitted or received.

quiz.q: If each layer has 4 switches, each switch has 24 ports, and 200 devices are connected, how many ports remain unused?
In a full mesh of 6 nodes, what is the total number of links?
Compare fault tolerance of a star and a ring topology when one link fails. Which continues to operate and why?
quiz.a: In a star, a single link failure isolates only the attached node; the rest of the network stays up because all other nodes communicate through the central device. In a ring, a single link break opens the loop, preventing any node from reaching others unless a bypass mechanism (dual ring) is present. Therefore the star has higher fault tolerance for a single link failure.

quiz.q: What formula gives the number of links in a full mesh with n nodes?

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern data‑centre networks use leaf‑spine partial meshes to achieve predictable latency and high bandwidth while keeping cabling costs manageable. Wireless mesh networks extend these ideas to outdoor deployments, for example in rural broadband projects. Researchers explore software‑defined topology control where logical topologies are re‑configured on demand. To see current practice, search for "Ethernet leaf‑spine architecture" and "Wi‑Fi mesh routing protocols".
